newsitem.title: USA: Intervention fears send dollar lower, sterling tumbles.
newsitem.headline: Intervention fears send dollar lower, sterling tumbles.

text.p: The dollar fell broadly on Wednesday, dropping to its lowest level in a month against the Japanese yen after a news report said Japan, the United States and Germany were conspiring to sell dollars for yen.

The one show of dollar strength was against the British pound, which fell sharply in late U.S. trading after a Bridge News report quoted an unidentified Labour Party source as saying sterling should join Europe's single currency in 2001 at a rate of 2.50 marks, well below its current 2.7790 mark level.

The U.S. currency shed a full yen, hitting a low of 124.60 yen after Japan's Kyodo news agency reported an unidentified international monetary source as saying the three nations were exploring the possibility of intervening in the foreign exchange markets to support the ailing yen.
The dollar has risen 10 percent so far this year against the yen, reaching a 56-month high of 127.47 yen on May 1.
The dollar closed at 124.97 yen, down from 125.38 at Tuesday's close, and 1.7191 marks, down from 1.7245, while sterling slid to $1.6135 from $1.6332.
Also depressing the dollar was a 139-point drop in the Dow Jones industrial average and a near full-point loss in the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond.

Sterling's steep slide demonstrated the currency markets' nervousness over the embryonic dollar policy of Britain's Labour Party, which ended 18 years of Conservative Party rule in last week's landslide election victory.

"The news story states that the Labour Party does in fact have a bias toward a weaker currency, not wanting to hinder employment from the export side," said David Durrant, senior currency strategist at consultants I.D.E.A.
"But they also want a little tighter interest rate policy, so they are on both sides of the fence," he added.
Britain raised its official interest rate 25 basis points on Tuesday. Higher interest rates usually cause a currency to appreciate.
Dollar volatility versus the yen was exacerbated by conflicting remarks from two Japanese Ministry of Finance officials over Japan's readiness to intervene and a surge in Japan's trade surplus.

MOF official Eisuke Sakakibara said it would be difficult to procure funds for intervention directly from the money market while another official told Reuters Japan can, if needed, use $220 billion of external reserves.

"If the Japanese do want to go forward with intervention, they have more than ample foreign exchange reserves to sell dollars," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer and Co.
Japan posted a customs-cleared trade surplus of 352.67 billion yen in the first 20 days of April, a swing from a 59.6 billion deficit in the same period last year.
There was no indication outside of Japan that intervention was being discussed. Officials at Germany's central bank and the U.S. Treasury declined to comment on the report.

The financial leaders of the three countries met in Washington at the end of April and released an official communique that called for foreign exchange rates to reflect fundamentals and said excess volatility was undesirable.

Traders also said the dollar's slip against the yen reflects diminishing prospects of higher official U.S. interest rates this month and signs that Japan may be preparing to raise interest rates, which currently are at historic lows.
In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.4584 Swiss francs from 1.4625 at Tuesday's close, but rose to Canadian $1.3819 from C$1.3783.
